# (PART) AI in measurement {-}

# Machine learning through an IRT lens {#ml-lens}

<div class="goals">
**Learning goals.** After this chapter you can

* explain the difference between a **prediction model** and a
  **measurement model**, and say what each can and cannot claim;
* show that a 2PL item response function is a logistic regression on a
  latent predictor, and what goes wrong when an observed score stands in for
  it;
* estimate how well a model predicts new cases with **cross-validation**, and
  recognize **overfitting**;
* explain why a single IRT score often predicts better than all the item
  responses fed to a flexible model.
</div>

**Key terms:**
[machine learning](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#machine-learning),
[feature](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#feature),
[overfitting and cross-validation](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#cross-validation),
[latent trait](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#latent-trait).
The [translation
table](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/ai-translation.html)
pairs many more machine learning words with their psychometric relatives.

## The ideas

Machine learning (ML) is a set of methods for learning a rule that predicts
an outcome from data. It is judged by one question: how well does the rule
predict cases it has not seen? Breiman [-@breiman2001] called this the
*algorithmic* culture of statistics, in contrast to the *data modelling*
culture that psychometrics grew up in, where a model is a claim about how the
data arose and its parameters mean something.

An IRT model makes such a claim. The 2PL says that the chance of a correct
answer depends on one unobserved trait through a logistic curve whose slope
and location are properties of the item. That is a logistic regression, with
one twist: the predictor $\theta$ is never observed. Everything that makes IRT
useful follows from taking that claim seriously: item parameters that do not
depend on who took the test, a standard error for every score, information
to design tests with, and checks of fit that can reject the model.

A prediction model makes a weaker promise. It does not say why the outcome
happens, only that its rule will predict well in data like the training
data. In exchange it can use any predictors (**features**) in any flexible
form. Two habits of ML are worth taking home even if you never fit a neural
network:

* **Hold data out.** A model always fits the data it was estimated on
  better than new data, and a flexible model can fit noise. This is
  **overfitting**, and the cure is to judge a model on data it did not see.
  **Cross-validation** splits the data into *k* parts (folds), fits the
  model on $k - 1$ of them, predicts the one left out, and repeats until
  every case has been predicted once [@james2021].
* **Shrink.** Penalizing large coefficients (ridge, lasso) trades a little
  bias for a large cut in variance. It is the same idea as a prior on item
  parameters, or as MAP and EAP scoring pulling extreme scores toward the
  mean.

Yarkoni and Westfall [-@yarkoni2017] make the case that psychology should
care more about prediction. The examples below show the reverse lesson as
well: a good measurement model is itself a very effective way to predict.

## Example 1: the 2PL is a logistic regression on theta

We simulate 20 items answered by 2,000 test takers whose true abilities we
keep, so we can do something impossible with real data: regress each item on
the true $\theta$.

```{r data-ml-lens-1}
# Simulated 20-item test with known abilities and item parameters.
set.seed(1313)
n <- 2000
theta <- rnorm(n)
a <- round(rlnorm(20, log(1.3), 0.3), 2)
b <- round(sort(rnorm(20, 0, 1)), 2)
p <- plogis(outer(theta, a) - matrix(a * b, n, 20, byrow = TRUE))
resp <- as.data.frame((matrix(runif(n * 20), n) < p) * 1L)
names(resp) <- sprintf("Q%02d", 1:20)
```

A logistic regression of item 5 on the true $\theta$ estimates its slope and
intercept directly; on the logit scale the intercept is $-ab$:

```{r}
fit5 <- glm(resp$Q05 ~ theta, family = binomial)
c(slope = unname(coef(fit5)[2]), b = unname(-coef(fit5)[1] / coef(fit5)[2]),
  true_a = a[5], true_b = b[5])
```

With real data we do not have $\theta$. The obvious stand-in is the sum score.
Doing the same regression on the standardized rest score (the sum of the
other 19 items) gives slopes that are on average about a fifth too flat,
because the rest score measures $\theta$ with error (Figure \@ref(fig:ml-attenuation)). IRT
avoids this by estimating $\theta$ and the item parameters together:

```{r}
mod <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
est <- coef(mod, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items
slope_obs <- sapply(1:20, function(j) {
  rest <- scale(rowSums(resp[, -j]))
  coef(glm(resp[[j]] ~ rest, family = binomial))[2]
})
round(c(true = mean(a), irt = mean(est[, "a"]), rest_score = mean(slope_obs)), 2)
```

```{r ml-attenuation, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "Item slopes estimated by the 2PL and by logistic regression on the standardized rest score, against the true slopes. The dashed line marks perfect recovery."}
slopes <- rbind(data.frame(true = a, estimate = est[, "a"], method = "2PL (mirt)"),
                data.frame(true = a, estimate = slope_obs, method = "Regression on rest score"))
ggplot2::ggplot(slopes, ggplot2::aes(true, estimate, colour = method)) +
  ggplot2::geom_abline(linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "True slope (a)", y = "Estimated slope", colour = NULL) +
  theme_mirtverse()
```

The lesson carries over to every ML model that uses test scores as
features: an observed score is a noisy measure of the trait, and models
that ignore the noise underestimate how strongly the trait relates to
anything else.

## Example 2: forty items or one score?

A university wants to predict which applicants will pass a first-year
statistics course from a 40-item placement test. We simulate 400 past
students whose course result depends only on their ability, plus noise.

```{r data-ml-lens-2}
# Simulated 40-item placement test and a pass/fail course outcome.
set.seed(2027)
n <- 400
ability <- rnorm(n)
a2 <- rlnorm(40, log(1.1), 0.3)
b2 <- rnorm(40, 0, 1)
p2 <- plogis(outer(ability, a2) - matrix(a2 * b2, n, 40, byrow = TRUE))
resp <- as.data.frame((matrix(runif(n * 40), n) < p2) * 1L)
names(resp) <- sprintf("P%02d", 1:40)
passed <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(1.6 * ability + 0.3))
```

The ML approach feeds all 40 item responses to a classifier as features.
The measurement approach first summarizes them in one IRT score and uses
only that. Both are logistic regressions here, so the comparison is about
the features, not the algorithm. We judge each by its accuracy on the data
it was fitted to and with 10-fold cross-validation:

```{r}
theta_hat <- fscores(mirt(resp, 1, verbose = FALSE))[, 1]
dat <- data.frame(passed, theta_hat, resp)
accuracy <- function(fit, newdata)
  mean((predict(fit, newdata, type = "response") > 0.5) == newdata$passed)

cv <- function(formula, k = 10) {
  fold <- sample(rep(1:k, length.out = nrow(dat)))
  mean(sapply(1:k, function(f) {
    fit <- suppressWarnings(glm(formula, binomial, data = dat[fold != f, ]))
    accuracy(fit, dat[fold == f, ])
  }))
}
items_formula <- reformulate(names(resp), "passed")
set.seed(1)
data.frame(
  features = c("40 item responses", "one IRT score"),
  training_accuracy = c(accuracy(suppressWarnings(glm(items_formula, binomial, data = dat)), dat),
                        accuracy(glm(passed ~ theta_hat, binomial, data = dat), dat)),
  cv_accuracy = c(cv(items_formula), cv(passed ~ theta_hat)))
```

On the training data the 40-item model looks better: with 41 coefficients
it can fit some of the noise. Cross-validation tells the truth. On new
students it does worse than the single score, because the IRT model has
already done what a good ML pipeline would have had to learn: that the
items measure one thing and should be combined with weights close to their
discriminations. A measurement model is a strong, theory-based form of
regularization.

This is not an argument against ML. With thousands of students, features
that carry information beyond the trait (response times, the text of
answers), or an outcome that depends on more than one trait, a flexible
model may well win. The point is to compare on held-out data and to know
what each approach is claiming.

## Your turn

<div class="yourturn">
1. In Example 1, repeat the rest-score regression using the EAP score from
   `fscores(mod)` instead of the rest score. Are the slopes closer to the
   truth? Why not?
2. In Example 2, change `n` to 2,000 in the data chunk and run the
   comparison again. What happens to the gap between the two approaches, and
   why?
3. Shrinking the 40 item coefficients toward a common value reduces
   overfitting; giving every item the same weight, the proportion correct
   `rowMeans(resp)`, is the extreme case. How does a model on the proportion
   correct do under cross-validation in Example 2?
4. A vendor reports that their ML model "predicts course success with 82%
   accuracy" from your placement test items. Write three questions you would
   ask before believing it.
</div>

<details><summary>Solutions</summary>

```{r}
# 1. the same regression on the EAP score of Example 1
resp1 <- extract.mirt(mod, "data")
eap <- fscores(mod)[, 1]
slope_eap <- sapply(1:20, function(j) coef(glm(resp1[, j] ~ eap, family = binomial))[2])
round(c(true = mean(a), eap = mean(slope_eap)), 2)

# 3. equal weights: the extreme form of shrinkage
dat$prop <- rowMeans(resp)
set.seed(1)
cv(passed ~ prop)
```

1. Now the slopes are too *steep* on average. EAP scores are shrunk toward
   the mean, so their spread is smaller than $\theta$'s and each unit of EAP
   corresponds to more than one unit of $\theta$; and each item's own response
   helped compute the EAP score it is regressed on. An estimated score is
   not $\theta$, whichever way you compute it; that is why IRT estimates the item
   parameters and the trait distribution together.
2. With 2,000 students the 40-item model has more data per coefficient, so it
   overfits less and the cross-validated gap narrows. It still rarely beats
   the IRT score, because the outcome depends only on the trait.
3. The proportion correct does about as well as the IRT score under
   cross-validation: equal weights are a strong form of shrinkage and lose
   little when the items' discriminations are similar.
4. For example: was the 82% computed on students who were not used to train
   the model? What is the accuracy of predicting from the total score alone,
   or of predicting that everyone passes? Is the accuracy similar for
   subgroups of students, such as English language learners?

</details>

## Further reading {-}

James et al. [-@james2021] is the standard introduction to statistical
learning, with R labs. Breiman [-@breiman2001] and Yarkoni and Westfall
[-@yarkoni2017] are short, readable arguments for taking prediction
seriously. Bulut et al. [-@bulut2024] survey where AI is used in
educational measurement.
